headline: A Builder Turns His Own Notes Into a Live Three.js Classroom
lede: Hasan built an interactive guide to Three.js, the dominant JavaScript library for 3D graphics in the browser, after finding that documentation alone kept sending him back to the same concepts. The guide hosts eight chapters — geometry, materials, cameras, lighting, scene objects, controls, post-processing, and a style gallery — each paired with a live playground the reader can manipulate in real time.
body:
**Three.js** is a JavaScript library that wraps WebGL (the browser's low-level graphics interface) into an API most web developers can actually use. Raw WebGL requires writing shader programs and managing GPU buffers by hand; Three.js abstracts that into objects like meshes, lights, and cameras. The library is used widely in interactive journalism, product visualizers, games, and creative coding — anywhere a web page needs to render something that feels spatial rather than flat.

The guide's distinguishing feature is not its topic list, which maps closely to any Three.js introduction, but its execution. Rather than static code snippets, each section embeds a scene the reader can drag and rotate, swap materials on, or push until something breaks. The author notes he spent more time building the playgrounds than writing the explanations — a disclosure that functions as both self-deprecation and thesis statement. The premise is that 3D graphics are genuinely hard to learn from prose alone: seeing a *MeshStandardMaterial* versus a *MeshPhongMaterial* requires light bouncing off a surface in real time, not a paragraph about physically-based rendering.

The post-processing chapter is worth singling out. Post-processing in Three.js refers to effects applied to the rendered frame as a whole — bloom (making bright areas bleed light), glitch, depth-of-field — rather than properties of individual objects. It is a common source of confusion because it sits outside the main render loop and requires its own pass-based pipeline. Having a playground that lets a learner toggle bloom intensity without setting up a local dev environment removes a significant friction point.

Hasan runs learnwithhasan.com, a broader content and tools site that also covers AI and business topics. The Three.js guide appears to be a genuine side project that grew out of notes accumulated while building his own 3D web work — a credible origin for a teaching resource, since the author has confronted the gaps firsthand. More sections are planned; the eight current chapters cover the core primitives but leave out topics like physics engines, custom shaders (*GLSL*), and animation systems.

concepts.definition: A JavaScript library that abstracts WebGL — the browser's low-level graphics API — into a friendlier object model of scenes, cameras, meshes, lights, and materials. It is the most widely used tool for 3D graphics on the web and runs entirely in the browser without plugins.

A browser API that gives JavaScript direct access to the device's GPU for rendering 2D and 3D graphics. It is powerful but low-level, requiring developers to write shader programs in a C-like language (GLSL). Libraries like Three.js exist largely to make WebGL approachable.

A shading model that simulates how light actually interacts with surfaces — accounting for roughness, metalness, and reflectance — rather than using simplified mathematical approximations. In Three.js, MeshStandardMaterial and MeshPhysicalMaterial are the PBR options; they look more realistic but are slightly more expensive to render.

Effects applied to a fully rendered image frame before it is displayed, rather than to individual objects in the scene. Common examples include bloom (bright areas bleed light), depth-of-field blur, and chromatic aberration. In Three.js these are handled via a separate EffectComposer pipeline layered on top of the main renderer.

repos.summary: The Three.js library itself, maintained primarily by Ricardo Cabello (mrdoob) and a large open-source community. It is the core dependency for the guide being described. At r184 as of mid-2026, it remains the dominant high-level 3D library for the web.
